questions.q: How far ahead should I book?
questions.a: Summer Saturdays go a year or more ahead. Fridays, Sundays and winter weddings, often a few months. Check your date on the cover.
A £150 booking fee, which comes off your total. Until then a date is only pencilled.

questions.q: When should I have my trial?
questions.a: Between six months and four weeks before. Your trial page works the dates out from your wedding.
Worked back from your ceremony: everyone else first, you last, with fifteen minutes spare. Before 7am there's an early-start fee.
On my own, up to six or seven before a 2pm ceremony. More than that, a second artist joins and we work two chairs.
Yes, by the hour until the speeches. Most brides take the touch-up kit instead.

questions.q: What if I have sensitive skin or allergies?

blocks.heading: Who goes first
blocks.body:
Everyone else sits before you: bridesmaids first, then mothers, so they're fresh for the photographs of you getting ready. You sit last, so your makeup is the freshest of the day, and you're finished fifteen minutes before your dress goes on.

Flower girls go whenever they're happiest, which is usually early, before they've been near the breakfast.

blocks.body:
We have your trial at the studio in London, as for any wedding. I fly out the day before, with the kit and a spare of everything that matters, and get you and your party ready on the morning. I fly back the day after.

Before you book, ask your venue whether it allows outside artists: most do, some charge for it.

items.title: Skin, the last twelve weeks
items.line: What to do, and what to stop doing, before your wedding, so your skin is ready for makeup on the morning.

photo.alt: A bride in profile fastening her earring: satin skin, warm brown eyes

blocks.heading: Keep it boring
blocks.body:
The best skin I see on a wedding morning belongs to brides who changed nothing. Twelve weeks out, settle on the cleanser and moisturiser you'll use on the day, and keep to them.

Four weeks out, stop trying anything new on your face, however good the review. A reaction takes days to calm down, and a wedding morning has none spare.

blocks.heading: The countdown
items: Twelve weeks: settle your routine
Eight weeks: your trial, with clean skin
Four weeks: nothing new
Ten days: the last brow shape and tint
The night before: your usual moisturiser, water and sleep
The morning: wash, a light moisturiser, nothing else

blocks.heading: Treatments
blocks.body: Peels, injectables and anything on prescription are a question for your clinician, not for me: ask them how long each needs before a day with photographs. Tell me at your trial what you've had, so I can work with it.

items.title: Until the last dance
items.line: Why bridal makeup stays put through tears, kisses and a long evening, and what's in your touch-up kit.

photo.alt: A bride laughing in profile, a pearl at her ear, hair swept back

blocks.heading: It starts with skin
blocks.body:
Makeup lasts when the skin under it is prepared, not when there's more of it. I prepare yours first, then build the base in thin layers and set each one, so it moves with your face instead of sitting on it.

Lashes are cut to your eye and placed with glue we patch tested at your trial. Mascara and liner are waterproof; you're allowed to cry.

blocks.heading: In your touch-up kit
items: Your lipstick or gloss, the one we used
Blotting papers
A powder puff and your powder
Cotton buds, for a tear in the wrong place

blocks.heading: When to touch up
blocks.body: After the ceremony and before the speeches: blot, then lip. That's all most brides need. For a very long day, I can stay until the speeches, by the hour.

items.title: Choosing your look
items.line: How to choose a bridal look you'll still love in the photographs: what to bring to your trial, and what to ignore.

photo.alt: A bride smiling between white curtains, a soft brown eye and lifted lashes

blocks.heading: Start with your face, not a photo
blocks.body:
Bring photos of looks you love, and just as useful, looks you don't. Then we look at what suits your face, your dress's neckline and the light you'll be married in. The best looks start as a photo and end up as you.

Wear a top with your dress's neckline to the trial. A high neck and a bare shoulder want different hair.

blocks.heading: Worth thinking about
items: Daylight or evening: the light changes how much the camera sees
Your veil or headpiece: hair is planned around it
How you wear makeup now: a step up, not a different person
Your photographer's style: soft and bright, or deep and moody

blocks.heading: Then live in it
blocks.body: After your trial, wear the look for the rest of the day. See it in a mirror at four o'clock, in a photo on your phone, in your partner's face. Then tell me what you'd change.
